key_terms.meaning: A network of identifiable physical things that sense, act and exchange data over networks to deliver services with little or no direct human control.
Any physical object that can be given a unique identity and connected to a network, such as a meter, a bulb or a wristband.
A part that converts a physical quantity (temperature, light, motion) into an electrical signal a circuit can read.
A part that converts an electrical command into physical action, such as a relay closing, a motor turning or a valve opening.
The small processor inside a device that reads sensors, runs the logic and drives actuators and the communication module.
The chip or board that sends and receives device data over a link such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee or NB-IoT.
The battery, mains supply or energy harvester that supplies a device with the energy it needs to run.
The fraction of time a device is active; average current = I_active × duty cycle + I_sleep × (1 − duty cycle).
A node that collects data from nearby low-power devices and forwards it to the internet over a different, usually wider, link.
One named job an IoT system performs, such as sensing or security, regardless of which hardware does it.
The function that gives every thing a unique name, address or tag (for example an IP address, a MAC address or an RFID tag) so data can be attributed to it.
The client sends a request and the server answers; the client must be connected and waiting for the reply.
Devices publish messages to a topic on a broker and other devices subscribe to topics; sender and receiver never connect directly.
The publisher pushes each value to a queue or broker, and the consumer pulls it later, so the two are decoupled in time.
A two-way link kept open between two parties for the whole conversation, so either side can send at any moment.
GET reads a resource, POST creates one, PUT replaces one, DELETE removes one; all act on a resource named by a URL.
An ordered set of layers or tiers showing where data is sensed, moved, processed and used in an IoT system.
Direct link between two machines for monitoring and control, usually without internet addressing, cloud services or people in the loop.
The sequence of players — chip makers, device makers, network operators, platform providers, system integrators, application providers — that together turn a connected thing into a paid service.
Delivering computing, storage, platforms or full applications as metered services instead of owned products.

takeaways: IoT is defined by three abilities together: identify each thing, sense or act on the physical world, and exchange data over a network with little human effort.
A physical device is only five parts — sensor, actuator, control unit, communication module and power source — and most design problems sit in balancing them.
The logical design names what the system must do; the physical design names what it is built from; exam answers need both.
Four communication patterns cover almost every IoT exchange: request-response, publish-subscribe, push-pull and the exclusive pair.
A layered architecture separates sensing, network, processing and application, so each layer can be replaced without rewriting the others.
IoT exists because cheap sensors, low-power radios, cloud storage and analytics matured at the same time and became affordable.
M2M is point-to-point control; IoT adds internet-scale addressing, cloud platforms, analytics and apps that people actually use.
Security, privacy, power, cost and device management are the recurring issues that decide whether a deployment survives.
Value in IoT is spread across a chain, and platform providers and service providers earn continuing revenue while device makers earn mostly once.
bank_note: Long answers are marked on definitions with an example, a labelled block diagram, comparison tables, and a clearly named layer or communication model tied back to a real deployment.

bank.q: Define the Internet of Things and explain its main characteristics with one Indian example for each characteristic.
outline: Definition: network of identifiable physical things that sense, act and exchange data to deliver services with little human control
Characteristics: connectivity, identity, sensing, actuation, heterogeneity, huge scale, dynamic change, energy constraint
Unique identification, e.g. IP address or RFID tag, so each meter's reading is attributable
Example: smart electricity meter reporting every 15 minutes so the discom bills correctly without a meter reader
Example: UPI-linked vending or IRCTC coach sensors
Contrast with plain internet of people: no human typing the data

bank.q: Explain the physical design of IoT. Draw a block diagram of an IoT device and state the function of each block.
outline: Definition of physical design: the actual things, devices and the parts inside them
Sensors convert physical quantity to electrical signal; name two types with quantity measured
Actuators convert command to action; relay, motor, valve examples
Control unit reads inputs, runs logic, drives outputs; microcontroller, memory, I/O
Communication module: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, NB-IoT and their trade-offs
Power source: mains, battery, solar, energy harvesting
Gateway role: collects from short-range nodes and forwards to internet
Labelled diagram with arrows from sensor to control unit to communication module

bank.q: List the functional blocks of a logical IoT design and explain what each one does.
outline: Definition of logical design: functions, not hardware
Identification: unique name or address per thing
Sensing: collecting data from the environment
Actuation: acting back on the environment
Communication: moving data between blocks over a link
Processing: filtering, aggregating, analytics, decision
Services: the four service types and what the user gets
Management: configuration, fault and device lifecycle control
Security: authentication, authorisation, integrity, confidentiality
State that the blocks may be on one board or split across device, gateway and cloud

bank.q: Explain the four IoT communication models with a diagram and an example of each.
outline: Request-response: client request, server reply, client waits; HTTP GET of a reading
Publish-subscribe: broker, topics, publishers and subscribers decoupled; MQTT example
Push-pull: publisher pushes to queue, consumer pulls later; analytics queue example
Exclusive pair: full-duplex connection kept open for the session; TCP-based control loop
Compare on: who initiates, whether both ends must be online, bandwidth, latency, power
One application of each from home automation or agriculture

bank.q: Differentiate M2M communication and IoT communication.
outline: M2M definition: direct machine-to-machine link for monitoring and control
IoT definition and what it adds
Comparison table: addressing, network, human interface, scale, analytics, cloud
M2M is usually closed and point-to-point; IoT uses IP and cloud platforms
Industry example from plant monitoring
One line on why the two overlap at the edge

bank.q: A housing society wants an overhead tank controller that measures water level and switches the pump, and reports to the cloud every five minutes. Select sensors, actuator, control unit, power source and communication model, and justify each choice.
outline: Sensor choice: ultrasonic or float switch for level, with reason
Actuator: relay or contactor driving the pump, with isolation note
Control unit: microcontroller with enough GPIO and a timer
Power source: mains with a small backup, or battery with duty-cycled radio
Communication: Wi-Fi through the society router, or NB-IoT if range is poor
Communication model: publish-subscribe to a broker topic for periodic reports
Local safety: dry-run cutoff and overflow cutoff must not depend on the cloud

bank.q: Design a REST API for a home automation system that can read and set the state of room lights. List the resources and show the GET, POST, PUT and DELETE calls.
outline: Resource naming: /lights and /lights/{id}
GET /lights returns the list with states
GET /lights/3 returns one light
PUT /lights/3 with a body of state replaces the state; safe for repeated calls
POST /lights creates a new light entry
DELETE /lights/3 removes it
Status codes 200, 201, 404 and their meaning
Note that REST here is stateless request-response over HTTP

bank.q: A battery-powered soil moisture sensor wakes for 2 s every 10 minutes, drawing 20 mA while awake and 0.02 mA while asleep. Compute the duty cycle and the average current, and explain two ways to extend battery life.
outline: Duty cycle = 2 s ÷ 600 s = 1/300 ≈ 0.0033, that is 0.33 percent
Average current = I_active × duty cycle + I_sleep × (1 − duty cycle)
Battery life ≈ capacity in mAh ÷ 0.087 mA, in hours, then divide by 24 for days
Extend by: fewer wake-ups, shorter active time, sleep the radio, send only on change, use a low-power link
Mention that waking the radio often costs more than the sensor itself

bank.q: Explain the three-layer and five-layer IoT reference models. Compare them and state where fog and edge computing fit.
outline: Three-layer model: perception, network, application, with the job of each
Limitation: no place for processing, management or security in the middle
Five-layer model: perception, transport, processing, application, business
Business layer: reports, billing, policy, model building
Edge computing sits at or near the device; fog sits between edge and cloud
Comparison table on number of layers, where processing happens and latency
Example: streetlight data processed at the gateway for switching, sent to cloud for billing

bank.q: A city plans 50,000 connected streetlights with fault reporting and dimming. Propose a communication model and an architecture, and justify the choices against cost, latency and power.
outline: Identify the traffic: small periodic status messages plus commands
Choose publish-subscribe over a broker, because many readers and independent topics
Architecture: perception at the pole, gateway or cellular link, processing in fog near the zone, application in cloud
Scale argument: 50,000 devices make per-client polling and request-response wasteful
Latency: dimming commands need a fast local loop, not a round trip to cloud
Cost: one gateway per group of poles versus one SIM per pole
Power: mains-powered poles relax battery limits but not radio congestion
Security: device identity, key provisioning and firmware update path

bank.q: Evaluate the claim that IoT is simply M2M communication with internet connectivity.
outline: What is true: both connect machines and carry sensor data
What IoT adds: unique IP-scale addressing, cloud platforms, analytics, human-facing apps
Scale difference: M2M is usually a closed point-to-point link
Data use: M2M acts on a reading, IoT stores and learns from many readings
Business difference: M2M is a one-time equipment sale, IoT is a subscription service
Verdict: M2M is a subset of patterns inside IoT, not a synonym

bank.q: Analyse the technical and social challenges of IoT in an Indian deployment, and suggest a mitigation for each.
outline: Security: weak default passwords, unencrypted links; mitigation: device identity, secure boot, updates
Privacy: continuous sensing in homes; mitigation: data minimisation, consent, local processing
Interoperability: many protocols; mitigation: gateways and standard APIs
Power and connectivity: unreliable supply and patchy coverage; mitigation: low-power wide-area links, buffering
Cost: device plus data plan plus platform fee; mitigation: shared gateways, XaaS pricing
Scale and device management: provisioning, monitoring, firmware upgrade of thousands of nodes
Standards and regulation still maturing
Social impact: deskilling, e-waste, surveillance

bank.q: Describe the IoT value chain and evaluate where value and revenue sit for each player. Explain XaaS in this context.
outline: Chain: component and chip makers, device makers, network operators, platform providers, system integrators, application and service providers, end users
Chip and device makers earn mostly per unit, with thin margins and short product lives
Network operators earn recurring connectivity revenue but face falling per-device rates
Platform providers earn recurring fees for device management, data storage and analytics
System integrators earn project revenue and lock-in through integration skill
Application providers earn subscriptions tied to a business outcome
XaaS shifts capital purchase to operating expense, e.g. monitoring as a service per month per device
Evaluation: recurring value sits with platforms and services, not with hardware

bank.q: Explain the enabling technologies of IoT and analyse which one limits a low-cost smart agriculture deployment.
outline: List: sensing and MEMS, embedded computing, wireless networking, cloud, big data and analytics
Note that none is new; the combination and the price fall made IoT possible
Sensing: cheap digital sensors with calibrated outputs
Embedded: microcontrollers with sleep modes and integrated radios
Wireless: trade-off of range, data rate and power; LPWAN versus Wi-Fi and Bluetooth
Cloud and analytics: storage, dashboards, prediction
Bottleneck analysis for farms: power, coverage and the cost of the data plan usually bind first
Conclusion: choose duty cycle, gateway placement and a low-power link to match the limit

glossary.def: A network of identifiable physical objects that sense, act and exchange data over networks to deliver services with little human control.
Any physical object that can carry a unique identity and be connected to a network.
The hardware assembly inside a thing that performs sensing, computation, communication and actuation.
A general element that converts one form of energy to another; sensors and actuators are both transducers.
A transducer that converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal.
A transducer that converts an electrical command into physical motion or switching.
The processor, memory and I/O that run a device's logic.
The radio or wired interface that carries device data to other nodes or the internet.
The battery, mains connection or harvester that supplies energy to a device.
The fraction of time a device is active; it drives average current and hence battery life.
A node that aggregates traffic from short-range devices and forwards it over a wider-area link.
A named function of an IoT system, independent of the hardware that implements it.
Assigning each thing a unique name, address or tag so its data can be attributed to it.
An interaction where a client sends a request and waits for the server's reply.
An interaction where publishers send messages to topics and subscribers receive matching topics through a broker.
The server in a publish-subscribe system that receives messages and forwards them to matching subscribers.
An interaction where the sender pushes messages into a queue and the receiver pulls them when ready.
A full-duplex connection kept open between two parties for the duration of a session.
An API style that treats data as resources named by URLs and acts on them with GET, POST, PUT and DELETE.
A reference model that splits an IoT system into ordered layers from sensing to application.
Processing data at or very near the device, before it travels to the cloud.
Processing in nodes between the edge and the cloud, such as a local gateway or zone server.
Direct machine-to-machine communication for monitoring and control, typically without cloud or human interaction.
Everything as a service: computing, platforms or full applications delivered as metered services.
The ordered set of players whose work together turns a connected thing into a delivered service.
Provisioning, configuring, monitoring and updating devices after they are deployed.
